prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "FREEPORT-MCMORAN INC" (ticker FCX), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "FCX", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Freeport-McMoRan Inc.
markets: Copper smelting and refining (Atlantic Copper, PT Smelting)

mission.source: Freeport-McMoRan 2024 Annual Report and 2025 Annual Report on Sustainability (stated objective)
mission.plain: Freeport wants to be the best and most important copper company in the world, supplying copper reliably and responsibly.

about.plain: Freeport-McMoRan digs copper out of the ground in giant mines in Arizona, Peru, Chile and Indonesia. Copper is the reddish metal used in electric wires, motors and pipes. Its Grasberg mine in Indonesia also produces a lot of gold, and its mines in the US produce molybdenum, a metal that makes steel stronger. It crushes and processes the rock and sells the metal to factories around the world.
about.customers: Smelters, refiners, wire and cable makers, steel mills and metal traders around the world.
about.everyday: The copper wires inside your home's walls, your phone charger and electric cars could well contain copper from a Freeport mine.

money.plain: Gold that comes out with copper at Grasberg
Moly for stronger steel and chemicals

money.part: Leach innovation (extra copper from old leach piles)
money.plain: New ways to get copper out of rock already mined

result.summary: Freeport's advantage comes from owning some of the world's largest, long-lived copper and gold deposits, such as Grasberg in Indonesia and Morenci in Arizona, which supplied about 7% of the world's mined copper in 2025. These cornered resources and its scale give it low costs (unit net cash costs of USD 1.65 per pound in 2025 against a realized price of USD 4.75), but it sells a commodity at market prices, so it has little pricing power.

pricingPower.evidence: Freeport sells at exchange-linked prices: its realized copper price rose from USD 4.54/lb in Q2 2025 to 6.17 in Q2 2026 with the market while its copper sales fell from 1,016M lbs to 710M lbs because of the Grasberg mud rush, and revenues swung from USD 14,198M in 2020 to 22,845M in 2021 with metal prices.

moats.evidence: Copper is a standardised commodity bought on specification and price, so the Freeport name does little to win customers.
Smelters and wire makers can buy copper concentrate or cathode from many miners and traders, though long-term offtake contracts and PT Smelting's tie to Grasberg add some stickiness.
A pound of copper is not more valuable to one buyer because others also buy from Freeport.

Huge deposits and by-product gold and molybdenum credits kept unit net cash costs at USD 1.65 per pound of copper in 2025 versus an average realized price of USD 4.75, though costs rose to USD 1.97 in Q2 2026 while Grasberg recovers.
New large copper mines take 10-20 years to permit and build and cost billions, so few rivals can add supply quickly in its regions (its Bagdad expansion needs about USD 4.00/lb copper to justify).
Its strategy of mining, expanding existing mines and leaching more copper is the same playbook rivals such as BHP and Southern Copper follow.

It runs one of the world's largest underground block-cave operations at Grasberg and its leach innovation added 101M lbs of copper in H1 2026, targeting a 300M lb annual run rate by end-2026, though the September 2025 mud rush showed the risks.

It controls world-class long-lived deposits such as Grasberg (Indonesia, with a February 2026 MOU to extend operating rights beyond 2041), Morenci and Bagdad (Arizona), Cerro Verde (Peru) and El Abra (Chile), together supplying about 7% of the world's mined copper in 2025.

customers.evidence: Buyers return for reliable supply under long-term concentrate and cathode contracts, but loyalty rests on contracts and availability rather than satisfaction; the 2025 Grasberg force majeure forced customers to find copper elsewhere.

talent.evidence: It is a large, well-paying employer in Arizona, Peru and Indonesia and ranked 2nd among mining and metals firms in the 2026 Corporate Human Rights Benchmark, but it has no notable employer-ranking awards and seven workers died in the 2025 Grasberg mud rush.

product.evidence: Its copper meets standard exchange grades like any other producer's, so the product is not best in class; its strengths are scale, reliability and a US-based supply chain (rod and refining in the US) valued under US critical-minerals policy.

competitors.name: Corporación Nacional del Cobre de Chile (Codelco)
competitors.note: Chile's state-owned miner, the world's largest copper producer, competing directly for copper sales.

competitors.name: BHP Group Limited
competitors.note: Owns Escondida in Chile, the world's largest copper mine, plus Spence and Copper South Australia.

competitors.name: Southern Copper Corporation
competitors.note: Large Peru and Mexico copper and molybdenum miner, a direct neighbour of Cerro Verde.

competitors.name: Glencore plc
competitors.note: Major copper miner and the largest copper trader, with mines in Chile, Peru, the DRC and Australia.

competitors.name: Zijin Mining Group Co., Ltd.
competitors.note: Fast-growing Chinese copper and gold miner with mines in the DRC, Serbia and South America.

competitors.name: Anglo American plc
competitors.note: Copper miner in Chile and Peru (Quellaveco, Los Bronces, Collahuasi stake), combining with Teck under a merger announced in 2025.

competitors.name: Teck Resources Limited
competitors.note: Copper miner in Chile, Peru and Canada (QB2), merging with Anglo American.

competitors.name: Antofagasta plc
competitors.note: Chilean copper miner (Los Pelambres, Centinela) competing for concentrate and cathode buyers.

competitors.name: Rio Tinto Group
competitors.note: Copper producer at Kennecott (Utah), Oyu Tolgoi and Escondida stake, also a US copper supplier.

competitors.name: CMOC Group Limited
competitors.note: Chinese copper, cobalt and molybdenum miner with large DRC copper mines; a major moly competitor.

competitors.name: First Quantum Minerals Ltd.
competitors.note: Copper miner in Zambia and Panama (Cobre Panamá, halted since 2023).

competitors.name: KGHM Polska Miedź S.A.
competitors.note: Polish copper and silver miner and smelter with mines in Chile and Canada.

competitors.name: Hudbay Minerals Inc.
competitors.note: Smaller copper producer in Peru and Arizona (Copper World project near Freeport's US mines).

competitors.name: Newmont Corporation
competitors.note: Largest gold miner, competing with Freeport's Grasberg gold sales; also a copper by-product producer.

estimates.name: Corporación Nacional del Cobre de Chile (Codelco)

marketShare.measure: tonnes of copper mined (Freeport's own estimate of about 7% of world mined copper in 2025; peers: company production / USGS 2025 world mine production of 23,000 thousand t, BHP on fiscal year to June 2026)

threats: Slow or troubled recovery of the Grasberg Block Cave after the September 2025 mud rush, which killed seven workers; operating rates are expected near full capacity only by end-2027
Indonesian government control: the PT-FI operating rights extension beyond 2041 is still being finalised and Freeport's stake would fall to about 37% from 2042
Copper and gold price falls, which hit revenues directly because Freeport has no pricing power
Rising unit costs (USD 1.97/lb in Q2 2026 versus 1.13 a year earlier) and capex overruns, such as Bagdad expansion costs now about 30% above the earlier USD 3.5B estimate
Fast-growing Chinese-owned miners such as Zijin and CMOC adding low-cost copper supply in the DRC and elsewhere
Trade policy and tariff uncertainty, plus tax, water and community issues in Peru, Chile and Papua

ceo.name: Kathleen L. Quirk
ceo.background: Louisiana State University graduate; joined Freeport in 1989 working in tax, investor relations, corporate development and treasury; CFO from 2003 and President from 2021

c1.evidence: Freeport is one of the world's largest copper producers, but copper mining is a centuries-old industry; demand is growing with electrification, yet Freeport's copper sales fell from 4,066M lbs in 2024 to 3,574M lbs in 2025.

c2.evidence: Customers buy its copper for reliable supply from large, long-lived mines like Grasberg and Morenci, an advantage rooted in geology that is hard to copy, but the product itself is a commodity sold at market prices.

c3.evidence: Investors and miners know Freeport as a top copper producer, but most ordinary people do not recognise the name and it is not the default leader the way Codelco and BHP are in size.

c4.evidence: Its stated objective 'Foremost in Copper' and its 'Accelerate the Future, Responsibly' strategy are repeated often, but they describe industry leadership rather than an inspiring purpose.

c6.evidence: “Copper, mining, Grasberg, Arizona” come to mind for those who know it; the impression is mixed, positive for supplying a critical metal but tarnished by environmental and community controversies in Papua and the deadly 2025 mud rush.

c7.evidence: Copper demand is large and expected to grow with electrification, power grids and data centres, and Freeport supplied about 7% of the world's mined copper in 2025.

c8.evidence: It can expand existing mines (El Abra mill expansion of over 700M lbs a year, Bagdad of 200-250M lbs) and leach technology targeting 300M lbs a year, but it stays tied to copper, gold and molybdenum.

m1.evidence: Kathleen Quirk has a clear plan to restore Grasberg, grow US copper through leaching and Bagdad, and extend Indonesian rights beyond 2041, but it is disciplined execution rather than a bold new vision.

m2.evidence: Quirk is a career executive who joined Freeport in 1989 and became CEO in 2024; she is not a founder.

m4.evidence: Freeport stresses safety and community programmes and ranked 2nd among mining and metals firms in the 2026 Corporate Human Rights Benchmark, but there is no clear evidence Quirk is known for servant leadership.

m5.evidence: Freeport has a strong technical culture behind block-cave mining and its leach innovation programme (101M lbs of extra copper in H1 2026), but this predates Quirk and is not a culture of new products.

m6.evidence: Quirk built her career in tax, investor relations, treasury and finance, serving as CFO from 2003, rather than in engineering or operations.

m7.evidence: Freeport emphasises responsible production and community investment in Papua and Arizona, but there is no clear evidence Quirk is known personally for causes beyond the company.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Quirk giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Quirk has a low-key, finance-focused public style and is not a widely known personality.

m9.evidence: As CFO and then CEO she helped cut debt and fund growth, and net income attributable rose to USD 2,204M in 2025 from 1,889M in 2024, but the 2025 Grasberg mud rush cut copper sales and raised costs.

m10.evidence: Freeport is cost-focused, keeping unit net cash costs at USD 1.65/lb in 2025, but it is not known for a distinctive frugal culture.

c10.evidence: Its copper ends up in wiring, power grids and electric vehicles used by billions of people, but it supplies a raw material rather than a product that directly improves lives.

p2.evidence: Running one of the world's largest underground block-cave mines at Grasberg in remote Papua and large open-pit mines in the Americas is very hard, and copper is critical to electrification.

f1.evidence: Revenues rose from USD 14,198M in 2020 to 22,845M in 2021, were flat at 22,780M in 2022, then rose to 22,855M in 2023, 25,455M in 2024 and 25,915M in 2025.

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 17.9% in 2020 to 38.6% in 2021 but then fell every year to 28.2% in 2025, and operating margin fell from 36.6% in 2021 to 25.2% in 2025.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026, consolidated debt of USD 9,386M was above cash of 4,080M but less than twice 2025 operating cash flow of 5,610M, and equity was positive at USD 30,766M at end-2025.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from USD 2,437M in 2020 to 6,518M in 2025 and operating cash flow from 3,017M to 5,610M, but both are below their 2021 peaks of 8,366M and 7,715M.

v1.evidence: Copper is a commodity, so buyers choose Freeport mainly for availability and contract terms, not because its copper is clearly better.

v2.evidence: Freeport does not appear in major best-places-to-work rankings, and safety concerns were highlighted when seven workers died in the 2025 Grasberg mud rush.

c5.evidence: Copper makers of wire, cable and electronics would notice the loss of about 7% of the world's mined copper, pushing prices up, but other miners would fill some of the gap and mining has environmental costs.
